conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your care team doctors. You're here for a planned surgery to remove a mass in your left temporal lobe. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Doctor. I’m a bit nervous, but okay. The headaches are still there—pressure at the back of my head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. The MRI before surgery showed the mass has grown, which is why we’re moving forward with the resection. We’ll monitor you closely after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my speech? I’ve been having trouble finding words since the last visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be related to the mass. After surgery, we’ll watch for any changes. Speech therapy will be involved if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, we’ve just finished the craniotomy. The surgery went well. We removed the mass safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good… I feel foggy. Can’t… find the right words.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re experiencing expressive aphasia—difficulty speaking. It’s common after this type of surgery. A CT scan shows no bleeding. We’ll keep monitoring you in the ICU.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noticed your sodium is low—125. It’s likely due to SIADH, possibly worsened by your blood pressure medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have diabetes insipidus too. Could that be involved?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We’ve paused your DDAVP for now because of the low sodium. We’re giving salt tablets and stopping hydrochlorothiazide. We’ll restart DDAVP once your sodium stabilizes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sodium is improving—127 now. We’re restarting DDAVP at a lower dose. Endocrine is helping us balance this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And the mass—any idea what it is?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Preliminary pathology suggests high-grade B-cell lymphoma. But we need to check if it’s only in the brain or elsewhere.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lymphoma? But I’ve had those enlarged lymph nodes for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, from your histiocytosis. But we need to be sure the lymphoma hasn’t spread. We’ll do a lymph node biopsy and bone marrow test.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your aphasia is improving. Speech therapy will start today to help with word-finding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried I’d never speak normally again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most patients recover well. We’re also watching your hepatitis B. Your viral load is undetectable, so no treatment is needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had chest pain yesterday when we flushed your line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, sharp pain in my right chest. Still a bit tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT didn’t show a clot or pneumonia. Troponin was normal. Likely musculoskeletal from the line. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CK was elevated after surgery but is now normal. That explains the muscle soreness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And the lymph node biopsy—when will we know?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s scheduled for tomorrow. We’ll target a node in your groin. Early looks suggest it’s not aggressive like the brain lesion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to do the lymph node biopsy. It’s ultrasound-guided and should take about 30 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll numb the area. You might feel pressure, but not sharp pain. We’ll get both aspirate and a small core sample.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Biopsy went well. Sample sent to pathology. We’ll do the bone marrow biopsy tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any word on EBV? I read it’s linked to lymphoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EBV tests show past infection—VCA IgG and EBNA positive, IgM negative. That’s common and not active disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Time for the bone marrow biopsy. It’ll be from your hip. We’ll use local anesthetic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: After my hip replacement? Will it be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use the opposite side. You should be fine. It’ll help us stage the lymphoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Biopsy complete. Minimal discomfort reported. Pathology pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we start chemotherapy—high-dose methotrexate. It’s strong, so we’ll give IV fluids, sodium bicarbonate, and monitor your levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I lose my hair? Feel sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hair loss is possible. We’ll give anti-nausea meds. Leucovorin rescue starts tomorrow to protect your cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Chemo infusion is complete. You tolerated it well. We’ll check methotrexate levels every 24 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel okay so far. Tired, but no nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your methotrexate level is dropping well. Leucovorin is helping clear it. Your aphasia continues to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We’ll send you home with leucovorin and sodium bicarbonate for one more day to finish clearing the chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Sodium is 127, normal for you now. DDAVP is well-titrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the seizures? I’m still on Keppra.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue levetiracetam twice daily. It’s controlling your symptoms well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding famotidine to protect your stomach from dexamethasone. And clonazepam for anxiety and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anxious. Thanks for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home. We’ll remove your central line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the lymph node and marrow results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Preliminary review shows lymphocytes but not aggressive like the brain tumor. Final results pending, but it looks like the lymphoma is confined to the CNS.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So just brain lymphoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. That means treatment can focus on the brain. You’ll continue with more chemo cycles as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my wife can help check the incision?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daily. Watch for redness, swelling, or drainage. Call if fever hits 101 or higher.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No lifting, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing over 10 pounds. Walk as you feel able. Speech therapy will continue at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds—dexamethasone, leucovorin, sodium bicarb for one day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Take them as prescribed. Stop hydrochlorothiazide. Continue lisinopril, DDAVP, and levetiracetam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. We’ll see you in follow-up. Rest, stay hydrated, and call with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—can I drink coffee?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but avoid carbonated drinks and vitamin C with meals—they can interfere with methotrexate clearance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No soda, no orange juice with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule your next chemo cycle soon. Rest up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep using the incentive spirometer at home—five times an hour while awake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep it by my chair.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re ready to be discharged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more—can I drive?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Wait for clearance at your follow-up. Use rideshare or family for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Discharge papers are ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. Patel, one of your oncology team doctors. You're here today for your second cycle of high-dose methotrexate for the brain lymphoma we diagnosed last month.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Doctor. Yes, I remember. I’m feeling much better since the surgery and the first chemo. My speech is back to normal, which is a huge relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent to hear. The aphasia you had after the craniotomy has clearly resolved, which is a very positive sign. We’ll be giving you the same dose today—6 grams per square meter—over several hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Last time I had some nausea afterward. Is that expected again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but we’ll give you anti-nausea medication as needed. We also start leucovorin 24 hours after the chemo to protect your healthy cells and help clear the methotrexate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the sodium bicarbonate? I remember that from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re giving IV fluids with bicarbonate to keep your urine alkaline, which helps your kidneys flush out the chemo safely. You’ll also take oral bicarbonate at home before your next cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my DDAVP for diabetes insipidus—I should keep taking that, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring your sodium closely. Your level was low on admission—127—so we’re holding DDAVP for now. We don’t want to worsen the hyponatremia, especially with all the IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t realize my sodium was low. Could that be from the DDAVP?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. It’s likely a combination—DDAVP, your history of SIADH, and the IV fluids. We stopped hydrochlorothiazide last time for this reason, and we’re being cautious now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. So when will I restart DDAVP?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once your sodium stabilizes and we stop the IV fluids. We’ll check it twice daily and let you know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my seizures—I’m still on levetiracetam?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 1000 mg twice daily. No changes there. We haven’t seen any seizure activity, and the involuntary movements you had before are gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about that. And my anxiety—I’ve been cutting back on clonazepam like we discussed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. We’ll keep you on 0.5 mg three times a day for now. As we taper the steroids, your anxiety may improve naturally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Steroids—aren’t I on dexamethasone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’re reducing it. From four times a day to twice daily—4 mg every 12 hours. This helps minimize side effects like mood changes and fluid retention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. When will the chemo start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In about 10 minutes. The nurse will set up the IV. It’ll take a few hours, so get comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another lumbar puncture or more biopsies?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not this time. The lymph node biopsy from your pelvis didn’t show cancer, just some abnormal lymphocyte changes. PET scan was negative, so we think the lymphoma is still confined to the brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. And my hepatitis B? I was worried about that flaring up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked—viral load is undetectable, no signs of active infection. You’re safe to proceed with chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. One less thing to worry about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your methotrexate infusion finished last night. We’ve started leucovorin this morning and will continue every six hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How’s my sodium today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It dipped a bit—120 this morning. That’s why we held DDAVP. But it’s moving in the right direction, and we’ll keep watching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At 120, we monitor closely, but you’re not showing symptoms like confusion or weakness. We’re adjusting fluids and holding DDAVP to let it rise safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. Any other labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is good—creatinine 0.8—and liver enzymes are stable. We’ll check your methotrexate level today to make sure it’s clearing properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the bicarbonate? I remember it made me a bit jittery last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the alkalosis from the bicarb. It’s expected and not harmful. We’ll keep an eye on your electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your methotrexate level is now undetectable. That means it’s cleared from your system, and you’re ready to go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What about my sodium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s still 120, but stable. We’ll restart your DDAVP at noon today and continue your usual dose at home. With IV fluids stopping, it should normalize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with leucovorin and sodium bicarbonate pills to take for a few days. Also, dexamethasone now twice daily instead of four times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need to remember that change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nurse will review everything with you. You’re doing very well—no nausea, no neurological symptoms, walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Your condition is stable, labs are acceptable, and you’ve completed the chemo cycle safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel ready to go home. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just continue the leucovorin and bicarbonate as prescribed. Watch for fever, confusion, or severe nausea—call us if those happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Oncology clinic in five days. We’ll discuss the next cycle and any adjustments. Keep taking DDAVP as before—two sprays morning and night, one at noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great. Keep up the good work, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You’re here today for your third cycle of high-dose methotrexate for your CNS lymphoma. How have you been feeling since your last treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Doctor. I’ve been doing pretty well overall. No seizures, no headaches. Just this mild fullness in my right ear that hasn’t gone away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. The ear fullness isn’t new, right? And you haven’t had any fevers, nausea, or dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. It’s just pressure, like when you’re on a plane. But otherwise, I feel stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep an eye on it, but it doesn’t sound concerning. You’ve been taking the sodium bicarbonate at home as instructed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, started yesterday morning—every six hours like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That helps protect your kidneys during the methotrexate infusion. We’ll continue IV fluids with bicarbonate too. You’ll get the chemo infusion around noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leucovorin? I remember that helps reduce side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ll get leucovorin starting later today and continuing over the next couple of days to help clear the methotrexate safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my DDAVP for diabetes insipidus—I’ve been using it as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep you on your regular DDAVP schedule. But we’ll monitor your sodium closely because IV fluids can dilute it. That’s been an issue in past cycles, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, last time my sodium dropped. I was a bit confused for a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check your sodium twice daily and adjust if needed. If it starts to drop, we may hold one dose of DDAVP, like we did before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. And my blood pressure and seizure meds are the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll stay on lisinopril and levetiracetam. No changes there. And we’ll keep your clonazepam and trazodone for anxiety and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The methotrexate infusion just started. It’ll run over the next few hours. How are you feeling so far?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No issues. Just a little nervous, but otherwise fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely normal. We’ll keep monitoring you. Let us know if you feel nausea, dizziness, or anything unusual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infusion is complete. You did great—no immediate side effects. We’ll start your leucovorin soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When will you know if the drug is clearing okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check your methotrexate level tomorrow morning. It should be down from the peak. We keep checking until it’s below 0.1, then we’re safe to discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my sodium? Any change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was 136 on admission—normal. We’ll check again tonight and tomorrow. We’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are back. Sodium is 130—slightly low. We’re going to hold your morning DDAVP dose to see if it stabilizes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I don’t want my DI to flare up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s just one dose. We’re giving you IV fluids, which can lower sodium, so holding DDAVP briefly helps balance it. We’ll restart it tomorrow if your sodium holds steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. Any other lab changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your methotrexate level is down to 0.11—excellent. That means it’s clearing well. One more level tomorrow, and if it’s below 0.05, we can plan for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. And my blood pressure? Still okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 128 over 74 this morning—perfect. You’ve stayed well-controlled on lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your leucovorin and IV fluids. You’re doing well overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling tired, but no nausea or pain. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, fatigue is common. Your body is processing the chemo. Rest as much as you need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your methotrexate level is now 0.04. That’s low enough for safe discharge. Your sodium is stable at 131.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll send you home on your regular DDAVP. But please get your sodium checked in a few days to make sure it stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Any other lab work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a full electrolyte panel—sodium, potassium, creatinine. Fax the results to Dr. ___’s office.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my dexamethasone? Still the same dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re tapering it down to 2 mg daily, as planned. That’s one tablet by mouth each day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can manage that. And the sodium bicarbonate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue one tablet every six hours starting 24 hours before your next admission. Same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for walking me through everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You tolerated this cycle very well. No complications, and your labs look good. We’ll see you in follow-up with neuro-oncology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I’ll make sure to get those labs done and call if anything feels off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Call us if you have nausea, confusion, or excessive urination. Otherwise, rest and take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in before discharge. All set for home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve got my meds and instructions. Ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great this admission. We’ll keep monitoring your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll follow up as instructed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Smith. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospitalists. You're here today for your high-dose methotrexate treatment for CNS lymphoma. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Doctor. I’m doing okay. Just the usual tinnitus, but nothing new or concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear you're feeling stable. We’ll be giving you methotrexate today after some IV fluids to protect your kidneys. You’ve been on this before, so you know the routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve done this many times. I brought my Temodar with me—I started it at home yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll make sure it’s documented. We’re also planning to place a Port-a-cath later this week to make future infusions easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. I forgot that was scheduled. Is it necessary? I mean, my veins have held up so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s safer and more comfortable long-term. With repeated chemo, veins can get damaged. This will give us reliable access and reduce discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. When will it be done?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Scheduled for Thursday morning. You’ll be under light sedation, and it usually takes about 20 minutes. No major risks, but we’ll monitor you after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I trust the team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started your IV fluids with sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize your urine. This helps clear the methotrexate safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Same as last time. Any changes in dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still 8 grams per square meter. Your body size puts it at about 19,360 mg. We’ll start the infusion in an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big number. But I know it’s targeted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And we’ll start leucovorin rescue 24 hours after to protect your healthy cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting the methotrexate infusion now. It’ll run over several hours. Let us know if you feel any nausea, chills, or discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ll let you know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your sodium is starting to drop—from 137 yesterday to 134 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a problem? I feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something we watch closely. Because you have diabetes insipidus and are on desmopressin, the large IV fluids can cause your body to retain too much water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the desmopressin is making it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Temporarily, yes. We may need to hold a dose to let your body correct the balance. We’ll check again in a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sodium dropped further—to 127. We’re going to hold your evening desmopressin dose and stop the IV fluids now that the methotrexate is cleared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel okay. But I trust you’re doing the right thing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are. We’ll give you a small dose of salt through the IV to help bring it up safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your sodium is improving. It’s up to 130 now. We’ll keep monitoring, but you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely tomorrow. We’ll check one more methotrexate level today. Once it’s low enough, and your sodium stays stable, you’re good to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Port-a-cath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still scheduled for tomorrow morning. You’ll go right after, once you’re awake and stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your last methotrexate level is 0.08—that’s excellent. It means the drug is cleared and you’re safe to stop leucovorin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. So I’m ready for the Port-a-cath and then home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The procedure team will see you tonight to go over consent, and you’ll have it first thing in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had the Port-a-cath placed successfully an hour ago. The catheter is in the right atrium, and it’s working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t even feel it. How’s the site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looks clean and dry. You’ll need to keep it dry for a few days, and we’ll check it at your next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid heavy lifting on that side for a week. Otherwise, you can resume normal activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. Your sodium is stable at 130, and you’re back on your regular desmopressin dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the low sodium was just from the fluids and desmopressin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It’s a common issue in patients like you. We managed it by holding fluids and a dose of desmopressin. It should stay normal now at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. What about the Temodar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue as prescribed—240 mg daily for seven days, then seven off. We’ve added ondansetron in case you feel nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had it before. Usually not too bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, take the sodium bicarbonate tablets the day before your next methotrexate—two every four to six hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same as before. I have it written down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with oncology in two weeks for your next methotrexate and rituximab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my eye check-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You said your ophthalmologist cleared you recently—no signs of intraocular lymphoma. Keep that follow-up as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all good there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. We’ll send all instructions and meds with you. Call if you have confusion, seizures, or severe nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Take care, and we’ll see you in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge—how are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really well. No headaches, no dizziness. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Your neuro exam is stable, blood pressure is good, and you’re walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been doing my walks every day here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That helps a lot. Keep it up. And remember—resume all your usual meds, including desmopressin, as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels home. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your labs from this morning show your liver enzymes were a bit high but are improving. Likely from the chemo, not a concern now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that before. They bounce back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll watch them, but no action needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your calcium and magnesium were low but corrected with supplements. We’ll check them next time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep taking the calcium pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please do. All set—discharge papers are ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , your oncologist. You're here today for your 19th cycle of high-dose methotrexate as part of reinduction therapy for your CNS lymphoma. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Doctor. I’m feeling okay—no headaches, no nausea, and no seizures lately. Just a bit tired, but I expected that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. We’ll be starting your methotrexate infusion today around noon. You’ll also continue your temozolomide at home starting tonight, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I brought my pills with me. I take 140 mg and 100 mg each night. Should I take them later today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll give you the dose tonight before bed. We also need to start sodium bicarbonate to protect your kidneys during the chemo. You’ll get that through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Is the methotrexate going to make me feel worse than usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some patients feel fatigue or mild nausea, but we’ll give you ondansetron if needed. Most tolerate it well, especially since you’ve had it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s reassuring. And my desmopressin—I take it three times a day for my diabetes insipidus. Will I still get that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll continue your desmopressin nasal spray. But we’ll monitor your sodium closely because the IV fluids and desmopressin can sometimes lower it too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time my sodium dropped. Was that why I felt so weak?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We caught it early. This time, we’ll check your labs frequently and adjust fluids if needed. No need to worry unless it drops again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. And my seizure meds—levetiracetam—I’ve been taking them regularly. Should I skip any dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, keep taking them as prescribed. We don’t want any breakthrough seizures. You said your last one was a few months ago?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I fell and lost consciousness. Scared me, but no injury. I’ve been careful since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep you on full seizure prevention. Also, your blood pressure is stable—139 over 82. You’re still on lisinopril?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 5 mg daily. No headaches or dizziness, so I think it’s working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll continue it. Any anxiety or trouble sleeping lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little anxious before chemo, but propranolol helps. I take trazodone at night if I can’t sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. We’ll keep those available as needed. I’ll see you again after the infusion starts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting your methotrexate infusion now. It’ll take a few hours. The nurse will monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I feel it going in. No discomfort so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your methotrexate level came back at 205—right on track. We’ll keep up the IV fluids and sodium bicarbonate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that high? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s expected this early. It’ll go down over the next few days. We’re watching it closely to make sure it clears properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my sodium? I remember it dropped last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs are back. Your methotrexate level is down to 0.08—that’s excellent. But your sodium is now 127.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s low again. Should I stop my desmopressin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold it for now and reduce your IV fluids. We’ll also give you some IV sodium chloride to bring it up safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my diabetes insipidus symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly—you might feel more thirsty or urinate more. But it’s temporary. We’ll restart desmopressin once your sodium is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can handle that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sodium is improving—now at 129. We’ll keep monitoring it. You’re doing well overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If your labs stay stable, likely tomorrow morning. We’ll check one more set of labs tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my next treatment? When is that scheduled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In about two weeks. Your oncology team will contact you to arrange it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to take anything special before the next dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just like this time—sodium bicarbonate the day before to protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your sodium is 127, stable, and your methotrexate level is 0.08. You’re cleared for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Do I restart my desmopressin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, go back to your usual three times daily. Keep an eye on your thirst and urination.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—everything else stays the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home medications continue as before—lisinopril, sertraline, levetiracetam, and temozolomide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about signs I should watch for? When to call?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you develop fevers, chills, numbness, dizziness, or any seizure-like activity. Also, if you feel unusually weak or confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with your neuro-oncologist. They’ll contact you to schedule it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did well this round. Rest up, and we’ll see you in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. Stay hydrated and keep up with your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your progress. Let us know if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’m grateful for the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re part of the team. We’re glad you’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I’ll see you next time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will assist you with discharge soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.text: What should it be at this point?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Because of my mom’s history?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was worried about that with the chemo weakening my system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: Nothing unexpected then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: Morning, Mr. ___. You’re ready for discharge. Your methotrexate level is 0.09, sodium is 137, and you’re feeling well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.text: And Temodar continues as planned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I come back here in two weeks for the next methotrexate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe. Depakote is often used for both seizures and mood stabilization. We’ll coordinate with your neurologist. But since you’re being discharged soon, you’ll start it at your next clinic visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. White count is a bit low at 3.4, but that’s expected with chemotherapy. Potassium is 3.7, so we’ll give you some oral supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? The low potassium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this level. It’s mild and common with IV fluids. We’ll replace it orally, and it should stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my sodium? I remember last time it dropped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sodium is 135—perfect. No signs of hyponatremia. We held your desmopressin this morning just to be safe, but you’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, right. Because of the fluid overload risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re giving a lot of IV fluid with the methotrexate, so we have to balance that with your diabetes insipidus treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting your methotrexate infusion now—19,680 mg over several hours. The nurse will monitor your urine pH to keep it alkaline, which helps clear the drug.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leucovorin starts tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 24 hours after the infusion ends. It protects your healthy cells from methotrexate. We’ll check your methotrexate level every morning until it’s low enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infusion is complete. You did well—no nausea, no reactions. We’ll keep an eye on your labs overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I’m feeling tired, but that’s normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your methotrexate level is 0.37—coming down as expected. Liver enzymes are slightly up, but that’s typical and temporary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any concern about my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. We monitor it closely. It usually recovers on its own after chemo. We’ll check again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my facial numbness? Still there, but not worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We still think it’s related to seizure activity. Keppra is helping some. You’ll follow up with Dr. Lee for an EEG soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, next week. I’ve been using medical marijuana at night—helps me relax.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just make sure it doesn’t interact with your other meds. We have you listed for cannabis use in your chart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is 102/62—lower than usual. You’re on lisinopril for hypertension. Should we adjust it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling a bit lightheaded. Maybe it’s too much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold it today and check again tomorrow. It could be from the fluids or the chemo. We’ll play it safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your methotrexate level is now 0.17. That means you can stop leucovorin and bicarbonate after today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m good to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ve tolerated everything well. No infections, no hyponatremia, no complications. We’ll discharge you this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my meds? Do I restart everything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—resume all your home medications, including desmopressin, lisinopril, Keppra, and temozolomide. Continue the Depakote plan with your neurologist at your next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up for MRI and Rituxan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same as before—Rituxan in three weeks, MRI surveillance in a month. Call us if you develop fever, confusion, or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did great. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I worry about TB? With the chemo and my history?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. You’re at higher risk, but your tests were negative, and we’ve been monitoring. Just stay alert for cough, fever, or weight loss—and report them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send your discharge papers shortly. Nurse will go over the instructions one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep using the medical marijuana responsibly—just know it’s not a substitute for your prescribed treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. It’s just for sleep and anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fair enough. Just keep your team informed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll sign the discharge order. Rest well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Thompson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the neurology team doctors. You're here today for your 27th cycle of high-dose methotrexate for your central nervous system lymphoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Doctor. Yes, I’ve been getting this treatment for a while now. Everything’s been going okay, but I hope we can proceed as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hoping so too. Before we start, we always check your blood counts to make sure it’s safe to give the chemotherapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I remember last time they were watching my potassium and sodium. Anything else we’re checking this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re also monitoring your liver and kidney function, and because of your history, we’re being cautious about infections, especially tuberculosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh right, because of my mom’s history. I forgot about that. Do you think I could get TB?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your risk is higher because of your chemotherapy, but your Quantiferon test was negative, which is reassuring. Still, we keep you in a special room until we confirm you’re clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, that’s why I’m in this room with the weird airflow. Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We just got your morning labs back. Your white blood cell count is a bit low—2.9, and it’s dropped to 2.7 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? Does that mean I can’t get the methotrexate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unfortunately, yes. We can’t give high-dose chemo if your white count is too low. It increases the risk of serious infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Why is it low? I felt fine coming in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be delayed effect from previous chemo, or something else. We need to rule out if the lymphoma has spread to your bone marrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. That sounds serious. So what happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discharge you today with an appointment for a bone marrow biopsy as an outpatient. Once we know what’s going on, you can come back for your treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s disappointing, but I understand. At least I’m not in danger right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re stable. Your other labs look good—kidneys, liver, electrolytes. Your physical exam is normal too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been having that tingling in my face again. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely seizure activity from the lymphoma. We’ve kept you on Keppra, and we’ve added a new medication—lamotrigine—to help better control it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lamotrigine? I haven’t taken that before. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We start low—25 mg twice a day. The main thing to watch for is a rash, especially in the first few weeks. If you see any, call us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll keep an eye out. And I should keep taking my desmopressin for the diabetes insipidus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Three times a day. And your blood sodium was good this morning, so that’s working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been drinking a lot, but at least I’m not passing out or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. We also checked a chest X-ray today to rule out TB, given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And? Is everything okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The X-ray shows old scarring from past infection, but no signs of active TB. So we can safely remove the airborne precautions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We were too. Your port was also switched from the right to the left side recently—everything’s healing well there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the new one feels fine. No pain or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Now, we’ll send your discharge papers and prescriptions. You’ll get lamotrigine, and continue all your other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lisinopril for blood pressure? Should I keep taking that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but monitor how you feel. Sometimes chemo can lower blood pressure. If you feel dizzy, let your doctor know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. And when should I expect the bone marrow biopsy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get a call from the oncology clinic within the next two days to schedule it. Once we have the results, we’ll plan your next admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll wait for that call. I just hope it’s not the lymphoma in the marrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hoping not. It could just be a lingering effect from treatment. Either way, we’ll figure it out and adjust your plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I appreciate you explaining everything. It’s a bit of a setback, but I’m ready to keep fighting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Stay in touch with the team, take your meds, and we’ll see you soon for the next step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning again, Mr. Johnson. I’m just stopping by before discharge to make sure you have all your questions answered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi Doctor. Yes, I think I’m all set. I’ve got the new prescription, and I’ll watch for any rash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Your repeat labs this morning still show the low white count, so our plan hasn’t changed. But everything else looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my seizures? The tingling hasn’t gotten worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. The lamotrigine should help over time. Keep taking it as prescribed, and keep using Keppra.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. And I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re cleared to go home. Someone will bring your discharge instructions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor. I’ll follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt? I’m a bit nervous about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s completely painless. Small sensors go on your scalp. You just need to stay still and maybe do some deep breathing. We won’t do hyperventilation because of your brain surgery history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds manageable. When will we know the results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. It’s like an antidote, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We also give sodium bicarbonate to protect your kidneys and lots of fluids to help flush the drug out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll drink plenty when I get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Almost. We want you to take a few doses of leucovorin and sodium bicarbonate here first to make sure you’re stable. You’ll continue them at home for three more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure I don’t miss any doses. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your usual medications continue—Desmopressin for diabetes insipidus, lisinopril for blood pressure, and Keppra for seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Lamictal? I’m on 25 mg twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing that to 50 mg twice a day. It’s an extra anti-seizure medication, and we want to keep building protection, especially with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll watch for any rash, like they told me last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s rare but important. If you see any rash, stop it and call us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I have a preliminary note on your EEG. It showed mild slowing in the left central temporal area, which is near your prior tumor and surgery site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? Does it mean I’m going to have another seizure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. It just shows some ongoing irritation or scar tissue in that area. The good news is no epileptiform discharges—those are the patterns that strongly predict seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the Keppra and Lamictal are doing their job?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and that’s why we’re keeping you on both. You’ve been seizure-free, and we want to keep it that way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show your white blood cell count dropped to 3.4, which is a bit low but expected after chemo. It’s not dangerously low, and it should recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not surprised. I just hope I don’t get sick. Should I avoid crowds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your methotrexate level is now 0.17, low enough for safe discharge. You’ve completed the critical part of the protocol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take leucovorin 40 mg every six hours for three days, sodium bicarbonate twice a day, and drink extra fluids. Continue all your regular meds, including the increased Lamictal dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have an appointment with Dr. Lee next week to review the final EEG and plan your next steps. We’ll decide then about future chemo cycles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care. I’ll follow the instructions carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Nurse will give you final instructions and your medication packets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
